title: The Peterkin Papers: The Lady Who Put Salt in Her Coffee
subject: English
description: Grammar-focused practice for the chapter: types of adverbs (manner, place, time) and choosing the right adverb, subject and predicate, subject-verb agreement (singular/plural, subjects joined by 'and', neither…nor, collective nouns), informal letter and diary entry writing, plus comprehension, characters, theme, glossary vocabulary and idioms from Lucretia Hale's 'The Lady Who Put Salt in Her Coffee'.

questions.question: What is an adverb?
options: A word that tells more about a verb
A word that names a person or place
A word that describes only a noun
A word that joins two sentences
questions.explanation: An adverb adds meaning to a verb (and sometimes to an adjective or another adverb). It tells how, where or when an action happens.

questions.question: An adverb of manner tells us ___ an action is done.
questions.explanation: Adverbs of manner answer the question 'How?' — e.g. 'worked tirelessly', 'stored carefully'.

questions.question: An adverb of place tells us ___ an action happens.
questions.explanation: Adverbs of place answer 'Where?' — e.g. 'gathered outside', 'waited here'.

questions.question: An adverb of time tells us ___ an action happens.
questions.explanation: Adverbs of time answer 'When?' — e.g. 'yesterday', 'next month', 'soon'.

questions.question: Which question does an adverb of manner answer?
questions.explanation: Manner = the way something is done, so it answers 'How?'. 'Where?' is place and 'When?' is time.

questions.question: Many adverbs of manner are made by adding which ending to an adjective?
questions.explanation: careful → carefully, quiet → quietly, safe → safely. The -ly ending is the most common adverb ending.

questions.question: 'The rescue teams worked tirelessly through the night.' The adverb 'tirelessly' is an adverb of ___.
questions.explanation: 'Tirelessly' tells HOW the teams worked, so it is an adverb of manner.

questions.question: 'Thousands of people gathered outside the town hall.' What type of adverb is 'outside'?
questions.explanation: 'Outside' tells WHERE the people gathered, so it is an adverb of place.

questions.question: 'Scientists will launch the satellite next month.' 'Next month' is an adverb of ___.
questions.explanation: 'Next month' tells WHEN the launch will happen, so it shows time.

questions.question: 'The young athletes ran fast and won three gold medals.' What kind of adverb is 'fast'?
questions.explanation: 'Fast' tells HOW the athletes ran. Note that 'fast' is an adverb that does not take -ly.

questions.question: 'The vaccine must be stored carefully.' 'Carefully' tells us ___.
questions.explanation: 'Carefully' describes the way (manner) of storing the vaccine.

questions.question: 'Yesterday, heavy rains flooded several towns.' Which word is the adverb of time?
questions.explanation: 'Yesterday' tells WHEN the rains flooded the towns.

questions.question: 'The chemist listened calmly to the story.' Which word is the adverb?
questions.explanation: 'Calmly' tells how the chemist listened — it is an adverb of manner.

questions.question: 'The lady from Philadelphia listened very attentively.' 'Attentively' is an adverb of ___.
questions.explanation: 'Attentively' tells HOW the lady listened — carefully and with full attention.

questions.question: 'Please wait here until I return.' What kind of adverb is 'here'?
questions.explanation: 'Here' tells WHERE to wait, so it is an adverb of place.

questions.question: 'We will visit Grandma tomorrow.' Which word is an adverb of time?
questions.explanation: 'Tomorrow' answers 'When will we visit?', so it is an adverb of time.

questions.question: 'The cat crept silently towards the bird.' Which word is the adverb of manner?
questions.explanation: 'Silently' tells how the cat crept.

questions.question: 'Come inside, it is raining!' What type of adverb is 'inside'?
questions.explanation: 'Inside' tells where to come.

questions.question: 'Soon the coffee grew cold.' What type of adverb is 'soon'?
questions.explanation: 'Soon' tells when the coffee grew cold.

questions.question: 'The herb-woman had gone up into the woods.' Which word is an adverb of place?
questions.explanation: 'Up' tells where she had gone. 'Woods' is a noun, 'gone' is a verb.

questions.question: 'The students answered politely.' 'Politely' tells us ___.
questions.explanation: 'Politely' describes the manner of answering.

questions.question: 'The little boys followed the others everywhere.' Which word is the adverb, and what type is it?
questions.explanation: 'Everywhere' tells WHERE the boys followed, so it is an adverb of place. 'Followed' is the verb and 'little' is an adjective.

questions.question: 'Mrs. Peterkin was sitting at breakfast alone.' What kind of adverb is 'alone'?
questions.explanation: 'Alone' tells HOW she was sitting (by herself), so it is an adverb of manner, even though it does not end in -ly.

questions.question: 'The dog barked loudly at night.' Which pair correctly names the adverb types?
questions.explanation: 'Loudly' tells how the dog barked (manner); 'at night' tells when (time).

questions.question: 'Rahul finished his homework early.' What type of adverb is 'early'?
questions.explanation: 'Early' tells WHEN he finished. Some adverbs of time, like 'early' and 'late', do not end in -ly.

questions.question: 'The chemist was down on his knees before his wife.' Which word is an adverb of place?
questions.explanation: 'Down' tells where the chemist was. 'Before' here is a preposition and 'knees' and 'wife' are nouns.

questions.question: 'They arrived late for the match.' Which type of adverb is 'late'?
questions.explanation: 'Late' answers 'When did they arrive?', so it is an adverb of time.

questions.question: 'She looked up and smiled sweetly.' Which option names both adverbs correctly?
questions.explanation: 'Up' tells where she looked (place) and 'sweetly' tells how she smiled (manner).

questions.question: Which sentence contains an adverb of TIME?
options: The children went upstairs to bed.
questions.explanation: 'Afterwards' tells when. 'Quietly' and 'together' tell how; 'upstairs' tells where.

questions.question: Which sentence contains an adverb of PLACE?
options: The boys searched eagerly for her.
The boys searched everywhere for her.
The boys searched again for her.
The boys searched slowly for her.
questions.explanation: 'Everywhere' tells where they searched. 'Eagerly' and 'slowly' are manner; 'again' tells when/how often.

questions.question: 'The herb-woman came round to sell herbs.' What type of adverb is 'round'?
questions.explanation: 'Came round' means she came around the neighbourhood — 'round' tells where she came.

questions.question: Which sentence means the student put in a lot of effort?
questions.explanation: 'Hard' is an adverb of manner meaning with effort. 'Hardly' means 'almost not', which is the opposite idea.

questions.question: 'Agamemnon sat himself down to do the sum.' Which word is an adverb?
questions.explanation: 'Down' tells where he sat — an adverb of place. 'Himself' is a pronoun, 'sum' a noun, 'sat' a verb.

questions.question: 'Elizabeth Eliza went immediately to the lady from Philadelphia.' 'Immediately' is an adverb of ___.
questions.explanation: 'Immediately' means 'at once' — it tells WHEN she went, so it is time, not manner.

questions.question: In which sentence is 'fast' used as an adverb?
questions.explanation: In 'ran fast', fast tells how they ran (adverb). In the other sentences 'fast' describes a noun or follows 'were', so it is an adjective.

questions.question: Select ALL the adverbs of time.
questions.explanation: 'Yesterday' and 'soon' tell when. 'Outside' tells where (place) and 'quietly' tells how (manner).

questions.question: Select ALL the adverbs of manner.
questions.explanation: 'Carefully' and 'gently' tell how. 'Nearby' is place and 'later' is time.

questions.question: Select ALL the adverbs of place.
questions.explanation: 'Upstairs' and 'everywhere' tell where. 'Already' tells when and 'safely' tells how.

questions.question: Select ALL the adverbs that do NOT end in -ly.
questions.explanation: 'Fast' and 'late' are adverbs with no -ly. 'Tirelessly' and 'attentively' end in -ly.

questions.question: 'Tirelessly' in 'the teams worked tirelessly' is an adverb of manner.
questions.explanation: It tells how the teams worked, so it is an adverb of manner.

questions.question: 'Yesterday' is an adverb of place.
questions.explanation: 'Yesterday' tells when, so it is an adverb of time, not place.

questions.question: An adverb of place answers the question 'When?'
questions.explanation: An adverb of place answers 'Where?'. 'When?' is answered by adverbs of time.

questions.question: The word 'here' is an adverb of place.
questions.explanation: 'Here' tells where something is or happens.

questions.question: Every adverb ends in -ly.
questions.explanation: Many adverbs end in -ly, but 'fast', 'hard', 'late', 'soon', 'here' and 'now' do not.

questions.question: In 'We met last week', the words 'last week' tell WHERE we met.
questions.explanation: 'Last week' tells WHEN we met, so it is an adverb of time.

questions.question: In 'She sang sweetly', the word 'sweetly' tells how she sang.
questions.explanation: 'Sweetly' describes the manner of singing.

questions.question: In 'They waited outside', the word 'outside' is an adverb of time.
questions.explanation: 'Outside' tells where they waited, so it is an adverb of place.

questions.question: The word 'alone' in 'she sat alone' is an adverb of manner.
questions.explanation: 'Alone' tells how she sat — by herself — so it is an adverb of manner even without -ly.

questions.question: 'Early' and 'late' are adverbs of manner because they describe the action.
questions.explanation: They answer 'When?', so they are adverbs of time.

questions.question: News report error: 'rescue teams worked loudly through the night'. Which word from the word bank corrects it?
questions.explanation: Rescue work is not about noise; 'tirelessly' (manner) shows how hard they worked all night.

questions.question: News report error: 'they will launch a new weather satellite yesterday'. What should replace 'yesterday'?
questions.explanation: 'Will launch' is in the future, so 'yesterday' does not fit. 'Next month' is a future adverb of time.

questions.question: News report error: 'young athletes ran fastly'. What is the correct word?
questions.explanation: 'Fast' is already an adverb; it never takes -ly. 'Fastly' is not a word.

questions.question: News report error: 'people gathered upstairs the town hall'. Which word is correct?
questions.explanation: People gather OUTSIDE a building; 'upstairs the town hall' makes no sense. 'Outside' is an adverb of place.

questions.question: News report error: 'it must be stored careful'. What is the correct word?
questions.explanation: 'Careful' is an adjective; the verb 'stored' needs the adverb 'carefully' (manner).

questions.question: News report error: 'Last week, astronauts landed tomorrow'. What should replace 'tomorrow'?
questions.explanation: 'Last week' and 'tomorrow' clash. The sentence needs to say HOW they landed — 'safely' (manner).

questions.question: Why is 'ran fastly' wrong?
options: 'Fast' is a noun, so it cannot change form
'Fast' is already an adverb and never takes -ly
'Fast' can only be used as an adverb of time
questions.explanation: Some adverbs, like fast, hard and late, have the same form as the adjective. Adding -ly to 'fast' is a common learner error.

questions.question: Why is 'stored careful' wrong?
options: An adverb is used where an adjective is needed
An adjective is used where an adverb is needed
questions.explanation: 'Careful' describes nouns; to describe the verb 'stored' we need the adverb 'carefully'.

questions.question: Why does 'Last week, astronauts landed tomorrow' not make sense?
options: 'Landed' should be in the future tense
'Last week' and 'tomorrow' are clashing time words
questions.explanation: You cannot land last week AND tomorrow. The sentence needs an adverb of manner like 'safely' instead of a second time word.

questions.question: What type of adverb was needed to correct 'gathered upstairs the town hall'?
questions.explanation: The correction 'outside' tells where people gathered, so an adverb of place was needed.

questions.question: How many of the six errors in the news report needed an adverb of MANNER to fix them?
questions.explanation: tirelessly, fast, carefully and safely are all manner (4); 'next month' is time and 'outside' is place.

questions.question: She is a careful driver. She drives ___.
questions.explanation: The verb 'drives' needs an adverb: careful + ly = carefully (one l before -ly, two l's total).

questions.question: He is a quick runner. He runs ___.
questions.explanation: To tell HOW he runs we need the adverb 'quickly'. 'Quick' is the adjective; 'quicker/quickest' compare.

questions.question: The adverb formed from the adjective 'happy' is ___.
questions.explanation: Adjectives ending in a consonant + y change y to i before adding -ly: happy → happily.

questions.question: The adverb formed from 'gentle' is ___.
questions.explanation: Adjectives ending in -le drop the e and add -y: gentle → gently, simple → simply.

questions.question: The adverb formed from 'angry' is ___.
questions.explanation: angry → angrily (y changes to i, then -ly is added).

questions.question: The adverb formed from 'terrible' is ___.
questions.explanation: Adjectives ending in -le drop the e and add -y: terrible → terribly.

questions.question: The adverb formed from 'true' is ___.
questions.explanation: 'Truly' is a spelling exception: the e of 'true' is dropped before -ly.

questions.question: The lady from Philadelphia listened ___ to the whole story.
questions.explanation: The verb 'listened' needs an adverb of manner: attentively. 'Attentive' is an adjective and the others are nouns.

questions.question: The children waited ___ for their mother's coffee.
questions.explanation: 'Waited' is a verb, so we need the adverb 'patiently' to tell how they waited.

questions.question: Which sentence uses an adverb of time correctly?
options: We will go to the park yesterday.
We went to the park next month.
We went to the park tomorrow.
We will go to the park tomorrow.
questions.explanation: 'Will go' (future) matches 'tomorrow'. The other sentences mix past verbs with future time words or future verbs with 'yesterday'.

questions.question: Which sentence about the boys is correct?
options: The boys climbed the rocks quickly.
The boys climbed the rocks quick.
The boys quick climbed the rocks.
The boys climbed quick the rocks.
questions.explanation: The verb 'climbed' needs the adverb 'quickly'. An adverb of manner usually comes after the verb or its object.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.
options: Riya did good in the spelling test.
Riya did well in the spelling test.
Riya did goodly in the spelling test.
Riya did well-ly in the spelling test.
questions.explanation: 'Well' is the adverb that goes with 'did'. 'Good' is an adjective; 'goodly' and 'well-ly' are not standard adverbs.

questions.question: Which sentence about the herb-woman is correct?
options: The herb-woman spoke soft to the children.
The herb-woman spoke softy to the children.
The herb-woman spoke softly to the children.
The herb-woman softly spoke the children.
questions.explanation: 'Spoke' needs the adverb 'softly'. The last option drops the word 'to' and so is not correct.

questions.question: Choose the sentence in which the adverb is placed correctly.
options: The chemist stirred slowly the coffee.
Slowly the chemist stirred slowly the coffee.
The chemist slowly stirred slowly the coffee.
The chemist stirred the coffee slowly.
questions.explanation: Adverbs of manner usually go after the verb and its object. Do not place it between the verb and its object, and do not repeat it.

questions.question: Which word completes the sentence correctly? 'The baby slept ___ all night.'
questions.explanation: 'Slept' is a verb, so we need the adverb 'peacefully'. 'Peaceful' is an adjective.

questions.question: Which word completes the sentence correctly? 'Astronauts landed ___ after six months in space.'
questions.explanation: The verb 'landed' needs an adverb of manner: 'safely'.

questions.question: Select ALL the words that are adverbs (not adjectives).
questions.explanation: 'Slowly' and 'bravely' are adverbs. 'Quick' and 'gentle' are adjectives; their adverbs are 'quickly' and 'gently'.

questions.question: Select ALL the words that can be used as adverbs WITHOUT adding -ly.
questions.explanation: 'Fast' and 'hard' keep the same form as adverbs. 'Quick' and 'careful' become 'quickly' and 'carefully'.

questions.question: Select ALL the correctly spelt adverbs.
questions.explanation: happy → happily and simple → simply. 'Easyly' should be 'easily', and 'fastly' is not a word (use 'fast').

questions.question: 'Fastly' is the correct adverb form of 'fast'.
questions.explanation: 'Fast' is both the adjective and the adverb. 'Fastly' does not exist.

questions.question: In 'stored careful', the word 'careful' should be 'carefully'.
questions.explanation: A verb needs an adverb, so careful → carefully.

questions.question: In the corrected news report, 'loudly' describes how the rescue teams worked.
questions.explanation: 'Loudly' was the error; the correct adverb is 'tirelessly'.

questions.question: The adverb formed from 'happy' is 'happily'.
questions.explanation: y changes to i before -ly.

questions.question: 'Good' is an adverb and 'well' is an adjective.
questions.explanation: It is the other way round: 'good' is an adjective and 'well' is the adverb (she sings well).

questions.question: An adverb of manner usually comes after the verb it describes.
questions.explanation: We say 'she sang sweetly', not 'she sweetly sang' (though some adverbs can move).

questions.question: 'Next month' is the correct replacement for 'yesterday' in 'will launch … yesterday'.
questions.explanation: 'Will launch' is future, so the time word must also be future: next month.

questions.question: The adverb formed from 'gentle' is spelt 'gentlely'.
questions.explanation: Adjectives ending in -le drop the e and add -y: gently.

questions.question: The subject of a sentence tells us ___.
options: what the subject does or is
who or what the sentence is about
questions.explanation: The subject names the person or thing the sentence is about; the predicate tells what the subject does or is.

questions.question: The predicate of a sentence tells us ___.
options: who or what the sentence is about
what the subject does or is
questions.explanation: The predicate is the part that contains the verb and tells about the subject.

questions.question: Which part of a sentence always contains the verb?
questions.explanation: The predicate contains the verb and everything that goes with it.

questions.question: 'The chemist added many strange chemicals to the coffee.' What is the subject?
questions.explanation: The sentence is about the chemist, so 'The chemist' is the subject; the rest is the predicate.

questions.question: 'The chemist added many strange chemicals to the coffee.' What is the predicate?
options: The chemist added many strange chemicals
many strange chemicals to the coffee
added many strange chemicals to the coffee
The chemist and the strange chemicals
questions.explanation: The predicate starts with the verb 'added' and tells what the chemist did.

questions.question: 'A large bird carried Gulliver's box high into the sky.' What is the subject?
questions.explanation: The sentence is about the large bird that did the carrying.

questions.question: 'A large bird carried Gulliver's box high into the sky.' What is the predicate?
options: carried Gulliver's box high into the sky
A large bird carried Gulliver's box
Gulliver's box high into the sky
A large bird high into the sky
questions.explanation: The predicate begins with the verb 'carried'.

questions.question: 'The kind lady from Philadelphia gave the family a simple idea.' What is the subject?
options: gave the family a simple idea
the family and the simple idea
The kind lady gave the family
questions.explanation: The whole group of words naming the lady is the subject; 'gave …' is the predicate.

questions.question: 'Mrs. Peterkin put salt in her coffee.' What is the subject?
questions.explanation: The sentence is about Mrs. Peterkin; 'put salt in her coffee' is the predicate.

questions.question: 'The little boys put on their India-rubber boots.' What is the predicate?
questions.explanation: The predicate starts at the verb 'put' and tells what the boys did.

questions.question: 'The old woman shook her head.' What is the predicate?
questions.explanation: 'Shook her head' tells what the old woman did.

questions.question: 'Solomon John shouted with joy.' What is the subject?
questions.explanation: The sentence tells us about Solomon John.

questions.question: 'The coffee tasted bad.' Which part is the predicate?
questions.explanation: 'Tasted bad' tells us about the coffee (what it was like).

questions.question: 'A brandy-cherry tree shaded the door.' What is the subject?
questions.explanation: The tree is what the sentence is about.

questions.question: Which of these is a complete sentence with a subject and a predicate?
options: The family sat down to think.
Down at the end of the street.
questions.explanation: Only 'The family sat down to think' has both a subject (the family) and a predicate (sat down to think).

questions.question: 'Elizabeth Eliza went to the lady from Philadelphia.' What is the complete subject?
questions.explanation: Elizabeth Eliza is the one who went; 'the lady from Philadelphia' is part of the predicate.

questions.question: 'The air in the garden was full of sweet smells.' What is the complete subject?
questions.explanation: The whole phrase naming what the sentence is about — 'The air in the garden' — is the complete subject.

questions.question: Which group of words is a PREDICATE, not a subject?
questions.explanation: A predicate contains a verb: 'tasted the salty coffee'. The other groups just name people — they are subjects.

questions.question: Which group of words could be a SUBJECT?
questions.explanation: Only 'the herb-woman's small parlour' names something; the others begin with verbs and are predicates.

questions.question: In 'Agamemnon, who had been to college, suggested the chemist', who or what is the subject?
questions.explanation: The sentence is about Agamemnon; the words between the commas describe him, and 'suggested the chemist' is the predicate.

questions.question: 'The children and Mrs. Peterkin made dreadful faces.' What is the subject?
questions.explanation: A subject can name more than one person joined by 'and'.

questions.question: Which sentence has the subject 'The chemist's wife'?
options: The chemist asked his wife for her ring.
The ring belonged to the chemist's wife.
The wife's ring was melted by the chemist.
The chemist's wife was just consenting.
questions.explanation: Only in the first sentence is 'The chemist's wife' the one the sentence is about and the doer of the verb.

questions.question: Add a predicate to make a sentence: 'The lady from Philadelphia ___.'
questions.explanation: A predicate must contain a verb: 'listened very attentively'. The other options have no main verb.

questions.question: Add a subject to make a sentence: '___ melted the gold thimble.'
questions.explanation: A subject names who did the melting: 'The greedy chemist'. The other options are not naming words.

questions.question: 'Down the street lived the herb-woman.' What is the subject?
questions.explanation: Even though it comes last, 'the herb-woman' is who the sentence is about — she is the one who lived.

questions.question: 'Into the parlour went the children.' What is the subject?
questions.explanation: The subject is the children (they went). Here the predicate part comes first for effect.

questions.question: In the command 'Make a fresh cup of coffee!', who is the understood subject?
questions.explanation: In commands the subject 'you' is not written but understood: (You) make a fresh cup.

questions.question: Which sentence has 'The coffee' as its subject?
options: Mrs. Peterkin could not drink the coffee.
The coffee tasted of anything but coffee.
The chemist stirred the coffee again.
Everyone tasted the coffee in turn.
questions.explanation: Only in the first sentence is the coffee the thing the sentence is about. In the others, the coffee is part of the predicate.

questions.question: Select ALL the complete sentences (each has a subject AND a predicate).
questions.explanation: 'The little boys' and 'Into the woods' have no verb, so they are not complete sentences.

questions.question: Select ALL the groups of words that are predicates.
questions.explanation: Predicates contain verbs: 'tasted …' and 'listened …'. The other two only name people (subjects).

questions.question: Select ALL the sentences where the subject is more than one word.
options: A large bird carried the box.
The kind lady gave an idea.
questions.explanation: 'A large bird' and 'The kind lady' are subjects of more than one word; 'Agamemnon' and 'Mother' are single words.

questions.question: The subject tells who or what the sentence is about.
questions.explanation: That is the definition of the subject.

questions.question: The predicate always comes before the subject.
questions.explanation: Usually the subject comes first and the predicate follows, e.g. 'The chemist | stirred the coffee'.

questions.question: In 'The children tasted the mixture', the predicate is 'tasted the mixture'.
questions.explanation: 'Tasted the mixture' tells what the children did.

questions.question: A predicate must contain a verb.
questions.explanation: The verb is the heart of the predicate.

questions.question: In 'A large bird carried Gulliver's box', the subject is 'Gulliver's box'.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'A large bird' — the box is what was carried (part of the predicate).

questions.question: In 'The coffee tasted bad', the subject is 'bad'.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'The coffee'; 'tasted bad' is the predicate.

questions.question: A subject can be made up of more than one word.
questions.explanation: E.g. 'The kind lady from Philadelphia' is one complete subject.

questions.question: In 'The chemist and his wife lived over the way', the subject is only 'The chemist'.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'The chemist and his wife' — two people joined by 'and'.

questions.question: In 'The chemist added chemicals to the coffee', the words 'to the coffee' are part of the predicate.
questions.explanation: Everything after the subject 'The chemist', including 'to the coffee', belongs to the predicate.

questions.question: The subject of a sentence is always a single noun.
questions.explanation: A subject can be a pronoun or a group of words, e.g. 'The kind lady from Philadelphia'.

questions.question: A singular subject takes a ___ verb.
questions.explanation: Rule 1: singular subject → singular verb (the book needs); plural subject → plural verb (the books need).

questions.question: Two subjects joined by 'and' usually take a ___ verb.
questions.explanation: Rule 2: 'The bag and the bottle ARE for my brother' — two subjects joined by 'and' are plural.

questions.question: A collective noun such as 'family' or 'group' takes a ___ verb.
questions.explanation: Rule 4: a collective noun names one group, so it is treated as singular: 'My family wants…'.

questions.question: With 'neither … nor', the verb agrees with ___.
options: the subject farther from the verb
the subject closer to the verb
the first noun in the sentence
questions.explanation: Rule 3: 'Neither the pens nor the marker IS in stock' — the verb agrees with 'marker', the closer subject.

questions.question: Letter to a store: 'My family ___ to order a few items.'
questions.explanation: 'Family' is a collective noun, so it is singular: wants (Rule 4).

questions.question: Letter to a store: 'The school bag and the water bottle ___ for my younger brother.'
questions.explanation: Two subjects joined by 'and' take the plural verb 'are' (Rule 2).

questions.question: Letter to a store: 'The notebooks ___ ruled pages.'
questions.explanation: 'Notebooks' is plural, so the verb is plural: need (Rule 1).

questions.question: Letter to a store: '… but the drawing book ___ plain pages.'
questions.explanation: 'The drawing book' is singular, so the verb is singular: needs (Rule 1).

questions.question: Letter to a store: '… if neither the red pens nor the blue marker ___ in stock.'
questions.explanation: With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the closer subject, 'marker', which is singular: is (Rule 3).

questions.question: Letter to a store: 'Our group of friends also ___ to order from you next month.'
questions.explanation: 'Group' is a collective noun and the real subject, so it is singular: plans — even though 'friends' is plural (Rule 4).

questions.question: The chemist ___ the coffee slowly.
questions.explanation: 'The chemist' is one person (singular), so the verb takes -s: stirs.

questions.question: The little boys ___ their India-rubber boots.
questions.explanation: 'Boys' is plural, so the verb is plural: wear (no -s).

questions.question: Mrs. Peterkin and her family ___ down to think.
questions.explanation: Two subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb: sit (Rule 2).

questions.question: The team ___ every evening after school.
questions.explanation: 'Team' is a collective noun, so it takes a singular verb: practises (Rule 4).

questions.question: The class ___ ready for the picnic.
questions.explanation: 'Class' is a collective noun — one group — so it takes the singular verb 'is' (Rule 4).

questions.question: Elizabeth Eliza ___ the only daughter in the family.
questions.explanation: One person = singular subject, so the singular past verb 'was' is used.

questions.question: The herbs ___ sweet and spicy.
questions.explanation: 'Herbs' is plural, so the plural verb 'smell' is used (Rule 1).

questions.question: Neither the chemist nor the herb-woman ___ the answer.
questions.explanation: With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the closer subject, 'the herb-woman' (singular): knows (Rule 3).

questions.question: Either the children or Elizabeth Eliza ___ to ask the lady.
questions.explanation: With either…or, the verb agrees with the closer subject, 'Elizabeth Eliza' (singular): goes.

questions.question: Neither Riya nor her friends ___ late today.
questions.explanation: The closer subject is 'her friends' (plural), so the verb is plural: are (Rule 3).

questions.question: The jar of herbs ___ on the top shelf.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'jar' (singular), not 'herbs'. Words between the subject and the verb do not change the agreement.

questions.question: The bags of catnip ___ from the ceiling.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'bags' (plural), so the verb is 'hang'. 'Catnip' is inside a describing phrase.

questions.question: Which sentence about the family is correct?
options: The family wants a cup of coffee.
The family want a cup of coffee.
The family wanting a cup of coffee.
The family are want a cup of coffee.
questions.explanation: 'Family' is a collective noun and takes the singular verb 'wants' (Rule 4).

questions.question: Which sentence about the two brothers is correct?
options: Agamemnon and Solomon John is brothers.
Agamemnon and Solomon John are brothers.
Agamemnon and Solomon John was brothers.
Agamemnon and Solomon John be brothers.
questions.explanation: Two subjects joined by 'and' take the plural verb 'are' (Rule 2).

questions.question: Which 'neither … nor' sentence is correct?
options: Neither the boys nor their sister were ready.
Neither the boys nor their sister are ready.
Neither the boys nor their sister was ready.
Neither the boys nor their sister be ready.
questions.explanation: The closer subject is 'their sister' (singular), so the verb is 'was' (Rule 3).

questions.question: Which rule explains 'The school bag and the water bottle are for my brother'?
options: A collective noun takes a singular verb
The verb agrees with the closer subject
A singular subject takes a singular verb
Subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb
questions.explanation: This is Rule 2: two subjects joined by 'and' are plural, so the verb is 'are'.

questions.question: Which rule explains 'My family wants to order a few items'?
options: A collective noun takes a singular verb
Subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb
The verb agrees with the closer subject
A plural subject takes a plural verb
questions.explanation: 'Family' is a collective noun (one group), so it takes the singular verb 'wants' (Rule 4).

questions.question: In 'neither the red pens nor the blue marker is in stock', the verb 'is' agrees with ___.
questions.explanation: With neither…nor the verb matches the subject nearest to it — 'the blue marker' (singular).

questions.question: Our group of friends ___ to the park every Sunday.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'group' (collective, singular), not 'friends', so the verb is 'goes' (Rule 4).

questions.question: Which sentence about the herbs is correct?
options: The herbs in the little bag smells spicy.
The herbs in the little bag is smelling spicy.
The herbs in the little bag was smelling spicy.
The herbs in the little bag smell spicy.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'herbs' (plural), so the verb is 'smell'. Do not let the singular 'bag' next to the verb trick you.

questions.question: Which sentence about the chemist and the children is correct?
options: Neither the chemist nor the children were happy.
Neither the chemist nor the children was happy.
Neither the chemist nor the children is happy.
Neither the chemist nor the children be happy.
questions.explanation: The closer subject is 'the children' (plural), so the plural verb 'were' is correct (Rule 3).

questions.question: Which sentence about the team is correct?
options: The team of players win the match.
The team of players wins the match.
The team of players winning the match.
The team of players are win the match.
questions.explanation: 'Team' is the subject — a collective noun — so it is singular: wins. 'Players' only describes the team.

questions.question: Which sentence has a subject-verb agreement ERROR?
options: The child goes to find the herb-woman.
The children go to find the herb-woman.
The children goes to find the herb-woman.
Solomon John goes to find the herb-woman.
questions.explanation: 'Children' is plural, so the verb should be 'go', not 'goes'. The other three sentences agree correctly.

questions.question: Which sentence about a trip has a subject-verb agreement ERROR?
options: My friends are planning a trip.
My family is planning a trip.
My friend is planning a trip.
My family are planning a trip.
questions.explanation: 'Family' is a collective noun and takes 'is' (Rule 4). The other three sentences are correct.

questions.question: Select ALL the sentences that are correct.
options: Neither Riya nor her friends is late.
questions.explanation: 'The boys climbs' should be 'climb' (plural). 'Neither Riya nor her friends is' should be 'are' (closer subject is plural).

questions.question: Select ALL the sentences in which the verb agrees with its subject.
options: The group of boys are ready.
questions.explanation: 'The lady listen' should be 'listens'. 'The group of boys are' should be 'is' (collective noun 'group').

questions.question: Select ALL the subjects that take a SINGULAR verb.
questions.explanation: 'Family' and 'group' are collective nouns (singular). 'The chemist and his wife' (joined by and) and 'the notebooks' are plural.

questions.question: Select ALL the sentences in which the verb correctly agrees with the CLOSER subject.
options: Neither the pens nor the marker is in stock.
Neither the marker nor the pens is in stock.
Either the boys or their sister goes first.
Either the sister or the boys goes first.
questions.explanation: In the first and third, the closer subjects (marker, sister) are singular, so 'is'/'goes' are right. In the second and fourth, the closer subjects (pens, boys) are plural and need 'are'/'go'.

questions.question: A collective noun like 'team' takes a singular verb.
questions.explanation: One team = singular: 'The team plays well' (Rule 4).

questions.question: Two subjects joined by 'and' take a singular verb.
questions.explanation: They take a plural verb: 'The bag and the bottle are new' (Rule 2).

questions.question: With 'neither … nor', the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it.
questions.explanation: That is Rule 3.

questions.question: 'The notebooks needs ruled pages' is a correct sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Notebooks' is plural, so the verb should be 'need'.

questions.question: 'Our group of friends plans a trip' is correct.
questions.explanation: 'Group' is a collective noun, so 'plans' (singular) is right even though 'friends' is plural.

questions.question: 'The children goes to school' is a correct sentence.
questions.explanation: 'Children' is plural: 'The children go to school'.

questions.question: 'Neither the boys nor their sister were ready' is correct.
questions.explanation: The closer subject is 'sister' (singular), so the verb should be 'was'.

questions.question: 'The boys and the dog is in the garden' is correct.
questions.explanation: Subjects joined by 'and' are plural: 'are in the garden'.

questions.question: 'Agamemnon and Solomon John were brothers' uses the correct verb.
questions.explanation: Two subjects joined by 'and' → plural 'were'.

questions.question: In 'The school bag and the water bottle are for my brother', the verb is plural because of the word 'and'.
questions.explanation: Rule 2: 'and' joins two subjects, making them plural.

questions.question: In 'Our group of friends plans', the verb agrees with 'friends'.
questions.explanation: The verb agrees with 'group', the real subject, which is a singular collective noun.

questions.question: In 'Neither the pens nor the marker is in stock', the verb is singular because 'marker' is closer to it.
questions.explanation: Rule 3: with neither…nor the verb agrees with the nearer subject.

questions.question: 'The jar of herbs are on the shelf' is correct because 'herbs' is plural.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'jar' (singular); 'of herbs' only describes it. The correct verb is 'is'.

questions.question: An informal letter is usually written to ___.
questions.explanation: Informal letters share news or feelings with people we know well, like friends and relatives.

questions.question: Which greeting (salutation) suits an informal letter?
questions.explanation: 'Dear Grandma,' is friendly and personal. 'Dear Sir/Madam' and 'Respected Sir' are used in formal letters.

questions.question: Which closing suits a letter to a friend?
questions.explanation: Informal letters end warmly: 'Your loving friend', 'With love', 'Yours lovingly'. 'Yours faithfully' is formal.

questions.question: Where is the date usually written in a letter?
options: At the very end, after the name
In the middle of the body
At the top, below the address
questions.explanation: The sender's address comes first at the top, then the date, then the salutation.

questions.question: What comes right after the salutation 'Dear Riya,' in a letter?
questions.explanation: After greeting the person, we begin the body — the main message.

questions.question: The L1 worksheet letter begins 'Dear Sir/Madam' and ends 'Yours faithfully'. What kind of letter is it?
options: An informal letter to a friend
A formal letter to a store
A diary entry for a shop
questions.explanation: 'Dear Sir/Madam' and 'Yours faithfully' are formal openings and closings; Riya is ordering from a store.

questions.question: Which sentence would fit best in the FIRST paragraph of an informal letter?
options: Kindly dispatch the items at the earliest.
This is to inform you of a complaint.
I hope you and Grandpa are keeping well.
Please find the invoice attached below.
questions.explanation: Informal letters usually start by asking about the reader's health and happiness in a friendly tone.

questions.question: Which tone is right for an informal letter?
questions.explanation: We write to friends and relatives the way we would talk to them — warmly and naturally.

questions.question: A student sharing a recent event with a cousin should end the letter with ___.
questions.explanation: A cousin is a relative, so a warm informal closing like 'Yours lovingly' or 'With love' is right.

questions.question: Select ALL the parts of an informal letter.
questions.explanation: A letter has an address, date, salutation, body, closing and name. Reference numbers and seals belong to official documents.

questions.question: Select ALL the closings that suit an informal letter.
questions.explanation: 'With love' and 'Your friend' are warm and informal; the other two are formal closings.

questions.question: An informal letter is written to a friend or relative.
questions.explanation: That is what makes it informal.

questions.question: 'Yours faithfully' is the usual closing for a letter to a friend.
questions.explanation: 'Yours faithfully' is formal; to a friend we write 'With love' or 'Your friend'.

questions.question: The sender's address and the date are written at the top of a letter.
questions.explanation: They come before the salutation.

questions.question: An informal letter must use very formal words such as 'kindly inform'.
questions.explanation: Informal letters use simple, friendly, everyday language.

questions.question: The body of the letter contains the news or event you want to share.
questions.explanation: The body is the main message of the letter.

questions.question: What is written at the top of a diary entry?
questions.explanation: A diary entry begins with the date, e.g. 'Monday, 5 May', so we remember when it happened.

questions.question: A diary entry is usually written in the ___ person.
questions.explanation: A diary records your own experiences, so you write 'I went…', 'I felt…'.

questions.question: Who is a diary entry written for?
questions.explanation: A diary is a private record of your own day, thoughts and feelings.

questions.question: Which opening is common in a diary entry?
questions.explanation: Many diary entries begin with 'Dear Diary,'. Formal salutations belong to formal letters.

questions.question: Which tense is mostly used in a diary entry about today's school day?
questions.explanation: You are describing things that already happened: 'Today we had a surprise test…'.

questions.question: Besides events, what should a good diary entry include?
questions.explanation: A diary is personal — it records not only what happened but how you felt about it.

questions.question: Which sentence belongs in a diary entry about an interesting day at school?
options: Kindly send the books by Friday.
Dear Sir, I wish to complain about…
I felt so proud when my team won the quiz!
questions.explanation: A diary entry is personal, first person and full of feelings. The others are formal letter sentences.

questions.question: How does a diary entry usually end?
options: With the writer's name or a short sign-off
questions.explanation: Diary entries end simply — with your name, or a line like 'Good night, Diary'. Formal closings are for letters.

questions.question: Select ALL the features of a diary entry.
questions.explanation: A diary is personal (first person) and dated. It is not addressed to anyone else and does not use formal closings.

questions.question: A diary entry records the writer's own day and feelings.
questions.explanation: That is the purpose of a diary.

questions.question: A diary entry must begin with the receiver's address.
questions.explanation: A diary has no receiver; it begins with the date.

questions.question: A diary entry is written in the third person, like 'She went to school'.
questions.explanation: It is written in the first person: 'I went to school'.

questions.question: Both an informal letter and a diary entry use a friendly, personal style.
questions.explanation: Both are personal forms of writing, unlike formal letters.

questions.topic: Story: The Salty Coffee and the Chemist
questions.question: What mistake did Mrs. Peterkin make?
options: She poured cream instead of milk
She put salt instead of sugar in it
She forgot to add sugar to her tea
She spilt the coffee on the table
questions.explanation: Just as she was adding cream, she found she had put salt in her coffee instead of sugar.

questions.topic: Story: The Salty Coffee and the Chemist
questions.question: What did the family do when they were called in?
options: Tasted, looked and sat down to think
Threw the coffee out of the window
Made a fresh cup straight away
Ran to fetch the lady from Philadelphia
questions.explanation: They all tasted, looked, wondered what should be done, and sat down to think.

questions.topic: Story: The Salty Coffee and the Chemist
questions.question: Who suggested asking the chemist?
questions.explanation: Agamemnon, who had been to college, said, 'Why don't we go over and ask the advice of the chemist?'

questions.topic: Story: The Salty Coffee and the Chemist
questions.question: Why did the family trust the chemist's advice?
options: He had already fixed their coffee
He was known as a very wise man
He owned the only shop in town
questions.explanation: The chemist lived over the way and 'was a very wise man'.

questions.topic: Story: The Salty Coffee and the Chemist
questions.question: What did the little boys put on before going out?
questions.explanation: Each time the boys went out, they put on their India-rubber boots.

questions.topic: Story: The Salty Coffee and the Chemist
questions.question: What was the chemist trying to discover?
options: Something to turn everything to gold
A medicine to cure every illness
A way to make coffee taste sweet
A machine for melting silver coins
questions.explanation: He wanted to find 'something which should turn everything it touched into gold'.

questions.topic: Story: The Salty Coffee and the Chemist
questions.question: Which item was the chemist asking for when the Peterkins arrived?
options: The gold head of a cane
questions.explanation: He had already melted the thimble, spectacles and cane head; now he was on his knees asking for her wedding ring.

questions.topic: Story: The Salty Coffee and the Chemist
questions.question: What did the chemist promise his wife in return for her ring?
options: A golden thimble and a cane
A new house of solid silver
A diamond ring set with jewels
A bottle of the finest coffee
questions.explanation: He promised a new wedding ring of diamonds set in emeralds, rubies and topazes.

questions.topic: Story: The Salty Coffee and the Chemist
questions.question: What is a crucible?
questions.explanation: The story explains: 'his crucible — that was the name of his melting-pot'.

questions.topic: Story: The Salty Coffee and the Chemist
questions.question: What did the chemist nearly do when the family burst in?
options: Throw his crucible at their heads
Lock the door and hide the gold
Pour the coffee into his bottle
questions.explanation: He was so mad that he 'came near throwing his crucible at their heads. But he didn't.'

questions.topic: Story: The Salty Coffee and the Chemist
questions.question: What finally made the chemist agree to help?
options: Mrs. Peterkin begged him to come
Agamemnon offered to pay in gold
His wife told him to go at once
He wanted to taste the coffee
questions.explanation: At first he refused, but when Agamemnon said they would pay in gold, he packed his bottles and went.

questions.topic: Story: The Salty Coffee and the Chemist
questions.question: What was the FIRST chemical the chemist put into the coffee?
questions.explanation: First he looked and stirred, then he 'put in a little chlorate of potassium'.

questions.topic: Story: The Salty Coffee and the Chemist
questions.question: What did the chemist add when he exclaimed 'I have it!'?
questions.explanation: 'I have it!' exclaimed the chemist, 'a little ammonia is just the thing!' — but it was not.

questions.topic: Story: The Salty Coffee and the Chemist
questions.question: What did Mrs. Peterkin say about the many acids the chemist tried?
questions.explanation: She tasted each and said the flavour was pleasant, but not precisely that of coffee.

questions.topic: Story: The Salty Coffee and the Chemist
questions.question: What effect did the tiny amount of arsenic have?
options: It gave the coffee a pretty colour
It made the coffee smell spicy
It turned the coffee to gold
questions.explanation: The arsenic 'gave rather a pretty colour', but Mrs. Peterkin said it still tasted of anything but coffee.

questions.topic: Story: The Salty Coffee and the Chemist
questions.question: After failing, what did the chemist say about his work?
options: The salt had been removed, though the taste stayed
The coffee was bewitched, so nothing could help
The theory remained the same, though the experiment failed
The family had added the wrong kind of salt
questions.explanation: He insisted that all he had done 'ought to have taken out the salt' — the theory was fine even though it failed.

questions.topic: Story: The Salty Coffee and the Chemist
questions.question: How much did the family agree to pay the chemist?
questions.explanation: They were willing to give him $1.37½ in gold; the herb-woman later took only five cents.

questions.topic: Story: The Salty Coffee and the Chemist
questions.question: Select ALL the items the chemist had ALREADY melted before the Peterkins arrived.
questions.explanation: The thimble, spectacles and the cane's gold head were melted. The wedding ring was only being asked for, and the furniture was a promise for later.

questions.topic: Story: The Salty Coffee and the Chemist
questions.question: The chemist asked his wife for her gold necklace to melt.
questions.explanation: He asked for her wedding ring.

questions.topic: Story: The Salty Coffee and the Chemist
questions.question: The chemist agreed to help the family for free.
questions.explanation: He only agreed when Agamemnon promised to pay in gold.

questions.topic: Story: The Salty Coffee and the Chemist
questions.question: The chemist could already turn things into pure gold.
questions.explanation: He could turn things into 'almost gold' — he had almost found what he wanted.

questions.topic: Story: The Herb-Woman and the Lady from Philadelphia
questions.question: Who suggested going to the herb-woman?
questions.explanation: Elizabeth Eliza said, 'Why don't we go to the herb-woman?'

questions.topic: Story: The Herb-Woman and the Lady from Philadelphia
questions.question: Elizabeth Eliza was named after ___.
questions.explanation: Elizabeth from her father's sister and Eliza from her mother's sister.

questions.topic: Story: The Herb-Woman and the Lady from Philadelphia
questions.question: Who was the herb-woman?
options: An old woman who sold herbs
questions.explanation: She was 'an old woman who came round to sell herbs, and knew a great deal'.

questions.topic: Story: The Herb-Woman and the Lady from Philadelphia
questions.question: Where was the herb-woman's house?
options: At the foot of a high hill
On top of the town hall
questions.explanation: It was at the very end of the street, 'at the foot of a high hill'.

questions.topic: Story: The Herb-Woman and the Lady from Philadelphia
questions.question: Why was the herb-woman not at home?
options: She was visiting the chemist's wife
She had gone to the woods for wild herbs
She was selling herbs in the town
She was asleep in her spicy parlour
questions.explanation: She 'had gone up into the woods to get some more wild herbs', so the children followed her.

questions.topic: Story: The Herb-Woman and the Lady from Philadelphia
questions.question: How did the children recognise the herb-woman?
questions.explanation: 'They knew her by her hat. It was steeple-crowned, without any vane.'

questions.topic: Story: The Herb-Woman and the Lady from Philadelphia
questions.question: What did the herb-woman put into the coffee first?
options: A little hop, for the bitter
questions.explanation: 'First she put in a little hop for the bitter.' Mrs. Peterkin said it tasted like hop-tea.

questions.topic: Story: The Herb-Woman and the Lady from Philadelphia
questions.question: What happened as the herb-woman added more herbs?
options: The coffee tasted worse and worse
The coffee began to smell of gold
questions.explanation: 'The more the old woman stirred, and the more she put in, the worse it all seemed to taste.'

questions.topic: Story: The Herb-Woman and the Lady from Philadelphia
questions.question: What did the herb-woman believe was wrong with the coffee?
questions.explanation: She shook her head, muttered a few words, and said she believed the coffee was bewitched.

questions.topic: Story: The Herb-Woman and the Lady from Philadelphia
questions.question: How much did the herb-woman take as payment?
questions.explanation: 'All she would take for pay was five cents in currency' — far less than the chemist.

questions.topic: Story: The Herb-Woman and the Lady from Philadelphia
questions.question: Who finally solved the problem?
questions.explanation: The lady from Philadelphia simply asked, 'Why doesn't your mother make a fresh cup of coffee?'

questions.topic: Story: The Herb-Woman and the Lady from Philadelphia
questions.question: Who went to ask the lady from Philadelphia?
questions.explanation: Elizabeth Eliza said, 'Suppose I go and ask her', and off she went alone.

questions.topic: Story: The Herb-Woman and the Lady from Philadelphia
questions.question: What did the lady from Philadelphia suggest?
options: Making a fresh cup of coffee
questions.explanation: 'Why doesn't your mother make a fresh cup of coffee?'

questions.topic: Story: The Herb-Woman and the Lady from Philadelphia
questions.question: What was Agamemnon doing just before the simple answer came?
questions.explanation: Agamemnon 'had just finished his sum' when he shouted with joy at the lady's idea.

questions.topic: Story: The Herb-Woman and the Lady from Philadelphia
questions.question: In what ORDER did the Peterkins seek help?
questions.explanation: First the chemist (Agamemnon's idea), then the herb-woman, and finally the lady from Philadelphia (both Elizabeth Eliza's ideas).

questions.topic: Story: The Herb-Woman and the Lady from Philadelphia
questions.question: Who went to find the herb-woman? Select ALL.
questions.explanation: Elizabeth Eliza, Solomon John and the little boys went; Mr. Peterkin and the chemist stayed behind.

questions.topic: Story: The Herb-Woman and the Lady from Philadelphia
questions.question: Select ALL the things the herb-woman carried.
questions.explanation: She took her trowel, her basket and her stick. The leather case and crucible belonged to the chemist.

questions.topic: Story: The Herb-Woman and the Lady from Philadelphia
questions.question: The children found the herb-woman digging round a sassafras bush.
questions.explanation: They saw her 'digging with her trowel round a sassafras bush'.

questions.topic: Story: The Herb-Woman and the Lady from Philadelphia
questions.question: The lady from Philadelphia lived at the end of the street.
questions.explanation: She was 'staying in town'; it was the herb-woman who lived at the end of the street.

questions.topic: Story: The Herb-Woman and the Lady from Philadelphia
questions.question: The herb-woman's hat had a weather vane on top.
questions.explanation: Her hat was steeple-crowned 'without any vane'.

questions.question: What is the central message of the story?
options: Simple common sense often solves problems best
Experts should always be paid in gold
Coffee should be made with herbs
questions.explanation: The chemist's chemicals and the herb-woman's herbs failed, but one simple idea — a fresh cup — solved everything.

questions.question: Who wrote 'The Peterkin Papers'?
questions.explanation: The story is signed '— By Lucretia Hale', an American writer who lived from 1820 to 1900.

questions.question: Why is the lady from Philadelphia wiser than the chemist?
options: She owns more gold than he does
She listens carefully and thinks simply
She has studied herbs for years
questions.explanation: The chemist knows a lot of science but has no common sense; the lady listens and thinks simply. Knowledge alone is not wisdom.

questions.question: What does the gold experiment tell us about the chemist?
options: He is generous and kind to his wife
He is poor and needs the money
He is lazy and avoids hard work
He is greedy and obsessed with experiments
questions.explanation: He is ready to melt his wife's wedding ring and family treasures, and only helps when paid in gold.

questions.question: If Mrs. Peterkin had been alone, how would the story probably have ended?
options: She would have made a fresh cup in a minute
She would have drunk the salty coffee
She would have called the chemist herself
She would have waited for the herb-woman
questions.explanation: The problem grew big because many people added complicated ideas; alone, she would likely have just made a fresh cup.

questions.question: A modern 'Peterkin problem': a phone won't switch on because the battery is empty. What is the Peterkin-style mistake?
options: Trying every complicated fix before charging it
Asking a neighbour for simple advice
questions.explanation: The Peterkins would call a repair shop, an expert and search online for hours before someone asks, 'Why don't you just charge it?'

questions.question: What makes the story funny?
options: The chemist turns the coffee into gold
The herb-woman casts a magic spell
Everyone misses an obvious answer for a whole day
Mrs. Peterkin drinks the salty coffee
questions.explanation: The humour comes from exaggeration — long lists of chemicals and herbs — while nobody thinks of simply making a fresh cup.

questions.question: Is the story really only about coffee? What else is it about?
options: Why herbs taste better than medicine
questions.explanation: The coffee is just a small example to make us laugh; the real lesson is to stay calm, think clearly and try simple solutions first.

questions.question: Which family member's suggestion led to the chemist, and what detail about him is given?
options: Agamemnon, who had been to college
Solomon John, who had been to sea
Mr. Peterkin, who read the newspaper
Elizabeth Eliza, who was the only daughter
questions.explanation: Agamemnon's college education is mentioned — yet even he did not think of the simple answer.

questions.question: Which word best describes the Peterkin family in this story?
questions.explanation: They try hard and mean well, but they are silly enough to miss the obvious solution all day.

questions.question: The story suggests that experts always know best.
questions.explanation: The 'experts' (chemist and herb-woman) failed; a simple, sensible idea won.

questions.question: Mrs. Peterkin had to wait the whole day for her cup of coffee.
questions.explanation: It was growing late in the day before the lady from Philadelphia's idea reached her.

questions.question: Agamemnon's college education helped him find the simple solution.
questions.explanation: Despite his college education, Agamemnon suggested the chemist and never thought of a fresh cup.

questions.question: In the story, 'consenting' means ___.
questions.explanation: The chemist's wife 'was just consenting' — agreeing — to give up her ring.

questions.question: 'Obliged' in 'they were all much obliged to him' means ___.
questions.explanation: The glossary defines obliged as thankful.

questions.question: 'Ungratefully' means ___.
questions.explanation: Mrs. Peterkin 'ungratefully said it tasted of anything but coffee' — she showed no thanks for the chemist's effort.

questions.question: What is a trowel?
options: A hat with a pointed top
A small hand tool for digging
questions.explanation: The herb-woman was digging with her trowel round a sassafras bush.

questions.question: 'Bewitched' means ___.
questions.explanation: The herb-woman believed the coffee was bewitched — charmed or enchanted as if by magic.

questions.question: 'Attentively' means ___.
questions.explanation: The lady from Philadelphia listened very attentively — carefully and with full attention.

questions.question: 'The chemist lived over the way.' What does 'over the way' mean?
options: At the end of the street
questions.explanation: 'Over the way' means just across the road — close enough to walk over at once.

questions.question: 'She had tried in vain' means she had tried ___.
questions.explanation: 'In vain' means without any success — the herb-woman's herbs did not help.

questions.question: Select ALL the glossary words that describe HOW someone did something (adverbs).
questions.explanation: 'Ungratefully' and 'attentively' are adverbs of manner; 'trowel' and 'crucible' are nouns (things).

questions.question: What is an idiom?
options: A phrase whose meaning differs from its words
A word that describes a verb
questions.explanation: An idiom's meaning cannot be worked out from the ordinary meaning of each word, e.g. 'a piece of cake' = very easy.

questions.question: 'Make a mountain out of a molehill' means ___.
options: to climb a very steep hill
to make a small problem seem huge
to dig a hole in the garden
questions.explanation: The Peterkins did exactly this — a cup of salty coffee became an all-day adventure.

questions.question: 'A piece of cake' means something that is ___.
questions.explanation: Making a fresh cup of coffee was a piece of cake — but nobody thought of it!

questions.question: 'Once in a blue moon' means ___.
questions.explanation: A 'blue moon' is rare, so the idiom means something that hardly ever happens.

questions.question: 'Add fuel to the fire' means ___.
options: to make a bad situation worse
to warm up a cold room
questions.explanation: The chemist added fuel to the fire — every chemical made the coffee worse instead of better.

questions.question: 'Back to square one' means ___.
questions.explanation: After the chemist and the herb-woman failed, the family was back to square one.

questions.question: 'Hit the nail on the head' means ___.
options: to say exactly the right thing
questions.explanation: The lady from Philadelphia hit the nail on the head with 'make a fresh cup'.

questions.question: 'Cost an arm and a leg' means ___.
questions.explanation: The chemist's fee in gold cost the Peterkins an arm and a leg compared with the herb-woman's five cents.

questions.question: Which idiom best describes the Peterkins' all-day fuss over one cup of coffee?
questions.explanation: A storm in a teacup is a big fuss about something small — exactly what the Peterkins made.

questions.question: Select ALL the idioms that mean something is EASY.
questions.explanation: 'A piece of cake' and 'child's play' both mean very easy. The other two mean a fuss about nothing and feeling unwell.

questions.question: 'Hit the nail on the head' means to hurt your thumb with a hammer.
questions.explanation: It means to say or do exactly the right thing.

questions.question: 'A piece of cake' means something very easy.
questions.explanation: It is one of the most common idioms for an easy task.

questions.question: The meaning of an idiom can be worked out from the ordinary meaning of each word.
questions.explanation: Idioms have special meanings — 'raining cats and dogs' just means raining heavily.

questions.question: 'Add fuel to the fire' describes what the chemist did to the coffee.
questions.explanation: Each chemical made the coffee worse — he made a bad situation worse.

questions.question: In which sentence is 'hard' an adverb of manner?
options: It was a hard test for her.
The hard rock hurt her foot.
She studied hard for the test.
questions.explanation: In 'studied hard', hard tells HOW she studied. In the other sentences 'hard' describes a noun, so it is an adjective.

questions.question: 'Mrs. Peterkin had not had her coffee yet.' What type of adverb is 'yet'?
questions.explanation: 'Yet' means 'up to now' — it tells about WHEN, so it is an adverb of time.

questions.question: 'So the little boys put on their boots, and over they went.' What type of adverb is 'over'?
questions.explanation: 'Over' tells WHERE they went — across to the chemist's house.

questions.question: Which sentence contains BOTH an adverb of manner and an adverb of place?
options: The boys climbed the rocks yesterday.
questions.explanation: 'Carefully' is manner and 'upstairs' is place. The other sentences use 'yesterday' (time).

questions.question: Which sentence contains BOTH an adverb of time and an adverb of manner?
questions.explanation: 'Yesterday' is time and 'beautifully' is manner. The others pair time+place, place+manner, or manner+manner.

questions.question: Which word in this list is NOT an adverb? quickly, loudly, lovely, softly
questions.explanation: 'Lovely' ends in -ly but it is an adjective (a lovely day). Not every -ly word is an adverb.

questions.question: Find the error: 'She speaks English very good.'
questions.explanation: 'Speaks' is a verb, so it needs the adverb 'well'. 'Good' is an adjective.

questions.question: Put the words in the best order: safely / the parcel / yesterday / arrived
questions.explanation: Adverb of manner (safely) usually comes right after the verb, and the time adverb (yesterday) goes at the end or the start.

questions.question: 'Friendly' is an adverb because it ends in -ly.
questions.explanation: 'Friendly' is an adjective (a friendly dog). The -ly ending alone does not make a word an adverb.

questions.question: In 'They came at last to the herb-woman's house', the words 'at last' tell WHEN they came.
questions.explanation: 'At last' means finally — an expression of time.

questions.question: 'Here she had marigolds and hollyhocks.' What is the subject?
questions.explanation: 'She' (the herb-woman) is who the sentence is about; 'Here' is an adverb of place and the flowers are what she had.

questions.question: 'Why don't we go to the herb-woman?' Who or what is the subject?
questions.explanation: The question is about 'we' — the Peterkins — going. 'The herb-woman' is part of the predicate.

questions.question: 'The coffee, which had gone cold, was thrown away.' What is the complete subject?
options: The coffee, which had gone cold
questions.explanation: The subject is the coffee, together with the words that describe it. The predicate is 'was thrown away'.

questions.question: Which sentence has 'went back with the children' as its predicate?
options: The children went back with the herb-woman.
The herb-woman went back with the children.
Back went the children with the herb-woman.
With the children went the herb-woman back.
questions.explanation: Only in the first sentence does the subject 'The herb-woman' do the action 'went back with the children'.

questions.question: In 'Over they went', the subject is 'they'.
questions.explanation: Even though 'over' comes first, 'they' is who the sentence is about.

questions.question: A cup of coffee ___ on the table.
questions.explanation: The subject is 'cup' (singular), not 'coffee', so the verb is 'is'.

questions.question: The flock of sheep ___ in the field.
questions.explanation: 'Flock' is a collective noun — one group — so it takes a singular verb (Rule 4).

questions.question: My brother and I ___ cricket every evening.
questions.explanation: Two subjects joined by 'and' take the plural verb 'play' (Rule 2).

questions.question: Which 'either … or' sentence is correct?
options: Either the pens or the marker are in stock.
Either the pens or the marker is in stock.
Either the marker or the pens is in stock.
Either the pens or the marker were being in stock.
questions.explanation: With either…or the verb agrees with the closer subject: 'marker' (singular) → is. In the second option the closer subject is 'pens', which needs 'are'.

questions.question: Which sentence about Monday meetings has a subject-verb agreement ERROR?
questions.explanation: 'Committee' is a collective noun and takes the singular verb 'meets' (Rule 4).

questions.question: In 'Riya and her brother are twins', the verb is plural because two people are joined by 'and'.
questions.explanation: That is Rule 2.

questions.question: 'Either the pens or the marker are in stock' is correct because 'pens' is plural.
questions.explanation: The verb agrees with the CLOSER subject, 'marker', which is singular: 'is in stock'.

questions.question: What is the correct ORDER of the parts of a letter?
options: Salutation, address, date, body, name, closing
Date, body, address, salutation, closing, name
Address, salutation, date, closing, body, name
Address, date, salutation, body, closing, name
questions.explanation: We begin with the sender's address and date, greet the reader, write the body, then close and sign our name.

questions.question: The L2 worksheet asks you to write a letter to ___.
options: a relative or friend about a recent event
a store manager about an order
questions.explanation: Worksheet L2, Part B: 'Write a letter to a relative or friend to share a recent event.'

questions.question: Where in an informal letter would 'Do write back soon!' usually appear?
options: At the top, before the address
At the end of the body, before the closing
questions.explanation: Friendly requests to reply come in the last lines of the body, just before 'With love' and the name.

questions.question: The L2 worksheet asks you to write a diary entry about ___.
options: a visit to a chemist's shop
questions.explanation: Worksheet L2, Part C: 'Write a diary entry about an interesting day at school.'

questions.question: Which line would NOT belong in a diary entry?
options: Today was such a surprising day!
I can't wait for tomorrow's match.
Dear Diary, you won't believe this.
questions.explanation: 'Yours faithfully' is a formal letter closing. Diary entries are personal and informal.
